claims.text: The starting alloy is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 with a bimodal grain-size distribution.
The starting W-Ta-Cr-V alloy develops Cr- and V-rich precipitates under irradiation.
Cr/V-rich precipitation in W38Ta36Cr15V11 occurs at approximately 8 dpa.
Irradiated W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening.
Approximately 3 at% Hf will be introduced to produce an alloy described as W31Ta34Cr15V11Hf3.
The Hf-modified alloy can be made using deposition followed by a bulk-consolidation route such as spark plasma sintering.
A W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf alloy has previously been irradiated with 400 keV Ar ions at 1073 K.
The cited irradiation precedent supports testing the proposed alloy at approximately 8 dpa.
Hf will segregate to grain boundaries or remain as a distributed solid solution.
Hf will reduce the grain-boundary mobility of Cr and V.
Hf reduces interfacial energy and retards grain-boundary atomic diffusion.
Restraining Cr and V mobility inhibits their co-segregation and subsequent precipitation.
Kinetic restraint of Cr and V mobility lowers the thermodynamic driving force for radiation-enhanced precipitation.
Adding Hf will lower the volume fraction of, or completely suppress, Cr/V-rich precipitates relative to the unmodified alloy.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain minimal irradiation-induced hardening.
Hf addition will maintain a stable single-phase microstructure under irradiation.
Enhanced structural stability from Hf will improve suitability for practical bulk or powder-metallurgy processing.
The proposed mechanism applies near 1073 K where diffusion permits segregation but remains susceptible to moderation by Hf.
TEM, APT, nanoindentation, and XRD measurements on irradiated base and Hf-modified controls can test the hypothesis.
Comparable or increased Cr/V precipitation, formation of deleterious phases, or significant hardening in the Hf-modified alloy would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as adding about 3 at% Hf to W38Ta36Cr15V11, but the stated modified formula W31Ta34Cr15V11Hf3 totals only 94 at% and changes W and Ta by substantially more than simple renormalization after a 3 at% addition.

The prediction of retained negligible irradiation hardening is opposed by the cited Hf-containing W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf result, in which hardness increased from 13.25 GPa before treatment to 20 GPa after irradiation at 1073 K and 10 dpa, although annealing and compositional differences complicate direct comparison.

The mediator is framed as a kinetic reduction in diffusion, whereas the mechanism claims that this kinetic restraint lowers the thermodynamic driving force. Reduced mobility can slow precipitation without necessarily reducing its thermodynamic driving force.
